raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a mechanical strategy for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF) that targets the principal anatomic source of thrombus in non-rheumatic AF. Autopsy, surgical, and echocardiographic series suggest that most thrombi in nonvalvular AF arise in or involve the left atrial appendage (LAA), whose trabeculated, contractile, and neurohormonal properties distinguish it from the smooth-walled left atrium [1,2]. The rationale for LAAC is therefore intuitive: exclude a thrombogenic cul-de-sac while avoiding the cumulative bleeding, adherence, interaction, and monitoring problems of long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC). Nevertheless, the therapy substitutes a lifelong pharmacologic risk for an up-front procedural risk plus residual risks of device-related thrombus, peri-device leak, and non-LAA embolic mechanisms.

The randomized evidence began with PROTECT AF, in which the first-generation Watchman device was noninferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, but with more early procedural complications [3]. Longer follow-up from PROTECT AF suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality versus warfarin [4]. PREVAIL, designed partly to test reproducibility and procedural safety, showed improved safety but did not meet all efficacy noninferiority criteria, largely because of unexpectedly low event rates in the control group [5]. Pooled 5-year data from PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported comparable overall stroke prevention to warfarin, with fewer hemorrhagic strokes, disabling/fatal strokes, cardiovascular deaths, and postprocedural major bleeding [6]. A randomized-trial meta-analysis integrating these studies with PRAGUE-17 reinforced the trade-off: similar ischemic protection, less hemorrhagic stroke and nonprocedural bleeding, and an early hazard related to the procedure [7].

The key contemporary question is not comparison with warfarin, but with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk patients—many with prior bleeding or embolism despite therapy—to LAAC or DOACs, predominantly apixaban, and showed noninferiority for a broad composite of ischemic, bleeding, cardiovascular, and procedural events [8]. Four-year follow-up preserved noninferiority and suggested less nonprocedural clinically relevant bleeding after LAAC [9]. In 2026, two larger randomized DOAC-era trials sharpened interpretation. CHAMPION-AF, enrolling anticoagulation-eligible patients treated with Watchman FLX, found LAAC noninferior to DOAC therapy for cardiovascular death, stroke, or systemic embolism and superior for nonprocedural bleeding at 3 years [10]. By contrast, CLOSURE-AF, enrolling older and higher-risk patients with elevated stroke and bleeding risk, did not establish noninferiority of LAAC to physician-directed medical therapy for a composite including major bleeding and cardiovascular or unexplained death [11]. These divergent results emphasize that patient selection, competing mortality, frailty, device generation, antithrombotic regimen, and endpoint construction materially influence apparent benefit.

Device evolution has been substantial. The Amulet IDE trial demonstrated that the Amulet occluder was noninferior to Watchman for safety and effectiveness and superior for LAA closure, albeit with different periprocedural profiles [12]; 3-year data showed sustained effectiveness and similar clinical outcomes [13]. SWISS-APERO, using cardiac CT surveillance, highlighted device-dependent differences in residual patency [14]. Watchman FLX was designed for improved recapture, sealing, anchoring, and deliverability; PINNACLE FLX reported high procedural success, low early major adverse events, and excellent 1-year anatomic closure [15]. Real-world experience with first-generation Watchman in EWOLUTION and U.S. continued-access and national registries confirmed high implant success in older, higher-risk patients, although event rates reflect substantial baseline comorbidity [16-20]. Amulet observational registries similarly demonstrated high implant success, acceptable early safety, and durable stroke rates below predicted risk in populations frequently unsuitable for long-term OAC [21,22].

Procedure planning typically combines transesophageal or intracardiac echocardiography with fluoroscopy, and increasingly cardiac computed tomography (CT) to define ostial dimensions, landing zone, depth, lobar anatomy, thrombus, and adjacent structures [23]. Standard implantation requires transseptal access, sheath positioning, device sizing, deployment, stability testing, leak assessment, and exclusion of pericardial effusion. Technical success alone is insufficient; the clinically relevant endpoint is durable endothelialized exclusion without thrombus or significant residual communication.

Postimplant antithrombotic therapy remains heterogeneous. Historical protocols used short-term warfarin plus aspirin, followed by dual then single antiplatelet therapy, but contemporary practice often uses DOAC-based, dual-antiplatelet, or abbreviated regimens tailored to bleeding risk [24]. Device-related thrombus occurs in a minority of patients but is associated with subsequent ischemic events and usually prompts intensified anticoagulation [25,26]. Peri-device leak, once considered acceptable below 5 mm, may carry incremental thromboembolic risk; CT detects residual patency more sensitively than transesophageal echocardiography and may refine follow-up strategies [27]. Observational data suggest low-dose DOAC strategies may reduce device-related thrombosis and bleeding in selected patients, but randomized evidence is still limited [28].

Guidelines now position percutaneous LAAC mainly for patients with AF, elevated thromboembolic risk, and contraindication to long-term OAC, and as a possible alternative in selected patients with high bleeding risk after shared decision-making [29,30]. In practice, the strongest candidates are those with substantial stroke risk, unacceptable or recurrent bleeding on OAC, limited competing noncardiovascular mortality, suitable LAA anatomy, and willingness to undergo surveillance imaging and short-term antithrombotic therapy. LAAC should not be framed as universally safer than DOACs; rather, it is a device-based risk-reallocation strategy whose value depends on individualized estimates of ischemic risk, bleeding risk, procedural risk, life expectancy, and patient preference.
